FOTO.about: The Tuttle Capital Pure Play Photonics ETF targets companies whose business is built around photonics: optical components, lasers, optical networking gear and the manufacturers behind them. Recent holdings have included names such as Lumentum, Coherent, Ciena, IPG Photonics and Fabrinet.
FOTO.watch: FOTO gets part of its exposure through total return swaps and holds a meaningful slice of cash and Treasury bills alongside those swaps, so its holdings list looks different from a plain stock basket. Check the issuer's latest holdings file to see how exposure is split between shares and swaps.
strategy: FOTO invests at least 80% of its net assets in photonics companies. To count, a company generally needs at least half of its revenue or operating profit to come from photonics, which is what the pure play in the name refers to. Tuttle describes five layers it draws from: lasers, transceivers, silicon photonics, specialty wafers such as indium phosphide, and the foundries and equipment makers behind them.

The fund leans toward small and mid-sized companies and can own foreign and emerging-market stocks. A manager picks the positions and sizes them, so the portfolio can change at any time without waiting for an index rebalance.
FOTO was the first U.S. ETF built only around photonics when it launched in late May 2026, and it is the base portfolio for Tuttle's weekly-pay income version, OPTO.
fit: You want a manager choosing among pure photonics names instead of an index formula
You want exposure that includes industrial laser makers such as IPG Photonics and nLIGHT, not only data center optics
You are comfortable with a fund that uses swaps for part of its exposure
notfit: You want the lowest fee in the group
You want a simple basket of shares with no derivatives
You want large chip-equipment names such as ASML or TSMC
risks: Swap exposure adds counterparty risk on top of stock risk
Small and mid-cap photonics stocks can fall 10% or more in a single day
Active funds can drift from what they held when you bought

holdings.note: Stock plus swap exposure combined. Cash and Treasury bills held as swap collateral are left out.

LYTE.about: The Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF focuses on the optical side of the AI infrastructure build: optical interconnects, lasers and photonic chips that move data with light inside AI data centers. At launch its top holdings included Lumentum, Coherent, Ciena and Fabrinet, plus China-listed optical module makers such as Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight.
LYTE.watch: A concentrated top ten and a large weight in China-listed optical module makers mean LYTE can move very differently from a broad semiconductor fund. Position sizes can change quickly in an actively managed fund.
strategy: LYTE puts at least 80% of its assets in companies whose core technology involves generating, manipulating, detecting or transmitting light. In practice it is a tight portfolio of the biggest optical names tied to AI data centers, with only about 18 positions.

It reaches the China-listed transceiver makers (Zhongji Innolight, Eoptolink and Suzhou TFC Optical) through total return swaps instead of buying the local shares directly. That is why its holdings file shows a large Treasury bill position: the bills back the swaps.
Roundhill says turnover should generally be limited to quarterly rebalances. The fund is non-diversified, which means a few names can make up a large share of the portfolio.
fit: You want the most concentrated bet on the largest AI optics names
You want exposure to the Chinese transceiver makers that supply much of the industry
You want a fund from a large thematic issuer with more trading volume than the smallest funds
notfit: You want to avoid China exposure
You want a wide basket; a handful of names drive most of the return
You want an index fund with fixed rules
risks: Three or four positions can make up more than half of the exposure
China-listed holdings add currency, policy and export-control risk
Swap exposure adds counterparty risk

holdings.note: Stock plus swap exposure combined. The Treasury bill held as swap collateral is left out.

LAZR.about: The Tema Photonics & Optical ETF invests in global photonics and optical technology companies tied to AI data movement, including optical interconnect, semiconductor technology and related equipment and materials. Tema launched it with research input from semiconductor analysis firm SemiAnalysis.
LAZR.watch: LAZR has also held a position in privately held AI company Anthropic, which is unusual for an ETF. Private positions are valued differently from listed stocks and can be harder to trade, so read the prospectus on how they are handled.
strategy: LAZR is a global, actively managed fund with about 25 holdings. It goes further up the supply chain than most of its peers: alongside Lumentum and Coherent it owns the companies that make the raw materials and tools for optical chips, such as Aixtron (deposition equipment), AXT (indium phosphide wafers), LandMark Optoelectronics and Win Semiconductors.
It is also the fund with the biggest single position in the group. Lumentum was more than a fifth of the portfolio in the issuer's November 2026 holdings file.

The fund can put a slice of its assets in private companies. Its largest private position is exposure to Anthropic held through a special purpose vehicle, which the issuer marks using secondary-market pricing.
fit: You want the materials and equipment layer of photonics, not only the module makers
You like a high-conviction manager willing to hold one large top position
You want a little private-company exposure inside an ETF wrapper
notfit: You want an even spread across holdings
You do not want private positions that cannot be priced daily on an exchange
You want a fund that sticks only to U.S.-listed stocks
risks: One stock above 20% of the fund means single-company news moves the whole ETF
Private holdings are marked by estimate and can be hard to sell
Foreign small caps in Taiwan, Germany and China add currency and liquidity risk

LUMA.about: The KraneShares Photonic and Optical ETF targets public and private companies worldwide that build optical interconnects, transceivers, fiber-optic cable and other light-based infrastructure for AI networking.
LUMA.watch: LUMA can hold private companies, IPOs and derivatives, and it carries one of the higher expense ratios in the group. That flexibility cuts both ways, so it is worth reading how the fund values and sizes its private positions.
strategy: LUMA is the most international fund in the group and the one with the most private-company exposure. Its largest position in the issuer's November 2026 holdings file was Ayar Labs, a private developer of optical chip-to-chip links, at about 12% of assets.

The public side of the portfolio spreads across Europe and Asia as well as the U.S.: Aixtron in Germany, Soitec in France, Eoptolink in China, Tower Semiconductor in Israel, LandMark in Taiwan and Nokia, next to Coherent, MACOM and Lumentum.
KraneShares describes the process as rules-based and research-driven. Position sizes are flatter than at LYTE or LAZR, so no single listed stock dominates.
fit: You want the widest global spread, including European photonics suppliers
You want meaningful private-company exposure to optical chip startups
You prefer flatter position sizes over one or two giant holdings
notfit: Fees matter most to you; this is the most expensive fund on the list
You want a large, heavily traded fund; LUMA is still small
You are not comfortable with a private company as the top holding
risks: A private company as the largest position is valued by estimate, not a market price
Small fund size can mean wider bid-ask spreads
The highest fee in the group is a guaranteed drag on returns

PHOX.about: The Aura AI Photonics ETF tracks the VettaFi AI Photonics Index, a basket of roughly 25 global companies involved in generating, transmitting and processing data with light for AI computing: lasers, transceivers, photonic integrated circuits and specialty materials such as indium phosphide.
PHOX.watch: As an index fund, PHOX follows set rules rather than a manager's calls, which makes it easier to know what you own. It is still a small, non-diversified, single-theme fund, so expect big swings.
strategy: PHOX is the only pure photonics ETF in the U.S. that tracks a published index. The VettaFi AI Photonics Index weights companies by how central photonics is to their business and by market value, then rebalances on a schedule.

The index reaches beyond the laser and module makers into the networking chips and connectors that sit next to them, which is why Broadcom, Arista, Credo and Amphenol show up in the top ten alongside Coherent, Lumentum and the Chinese transceiver makers.
Because the rules are public, you can see ahead of time what the fund will own and when it will change. The trade-off is that nobody is steering around a problem stock between rebalances.
fit: You want fixed, published rules instead of a manager's judgment
You want a flatter spread across the top ten than the active funds offer
You want optical networking names such as Broadcom, Arista and Credo in the mix
notfit: You need a fund with heavy daily trading volume; PHOX is very small
You want only pure photonics companies; several holdings are broader networking names
You want to avoid China-listed stocks
risks: Very small funds can trade at wide spreads and face closure risk if they do not grow
Index rules can force buying after big run-ups
China-listed holdings add policy and currency risk

EUV.about: The Corgi Lithography & Semiconductor Photonics ETF takes a wider angle on photonics, centered on lithography and chipmaking: the light-based tools that print chips, the equipment makers around them and the foundries that use them. Large positions have included ASML, TSMC, Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA.
EUV.watch: Because it leans on large semiconductor equipment and foundry names, EUV behaves more like a chip-equipment fund than a pure optical networking fund. That can make it steadier than the pure plays, but it is a different bet.
strategy: EUV is named after extreme ultraviolet lithography, the process that uses 13.5-nanometer light to print the smallest features on advanced chips. The fund starts there, with ASML and the foundry that buys the most of its machines, TSMC, then adds the big U.S. equipment makers.
Optical networking is a smaller sleeve. Corning, Lumentum, Coherent and Ciena all appeared in the top ten in the issuer's November 2026 holdings, each at roughly 3% to 4%.
It is the cheapest photonics ETF and the one built from the largest companies, which is a big reason it has gathered more assets than most of the group.
fit: You want the lowest fee among photonics ETFs
You want large, established chip-equipment companies with a smaller optical sleeve
You want photonics exposure with less small-cap swing
notfit: You want a pure optical networking fund; this is mostly chip equipment
You already own a semiconductor ETF and want something that does not overlap much with it
You want the companies most directly tied to AI data center optics
risks: Heavy overlap with semiconductor equipment funds
TSMC and ASML together are close to a quarter of the fund
Chip-equipment spending is cyclical and sensitive to export controls

EUVX.index: None (targets 2x the daily move of EUV)
EUVX.about: The Corgi Lithography & Semiconductor Photonics 2x Daily ETF aims for twice the daily move of its lithography and semiconductor photonics strategy.
EUVX.watch: Leveraged ETFs reset every day. Over periods longer than a day, returns can differ a lot from 2x the underlying move, especially in choppy markets. These are trading tools, not long-term holdings for most investors.
strategy: EUVX does not own a basket of stocks. It holds a total return swap that references the unleveraged EUV fund, sized at roughly 200% of assets, with cash and Treasury holdings behind it.
The goal is twice the return of EUV for a single day. The fund rebalances its swap exposure at the end of every trading day to get back to 2x.

That daily reset is why the long-run result is not simply double. If EUV falls 10% one day and rises 10% the next, EUV is down 1% while a 2x fund is down 4%. The more the underlying fund whipsaws, the wider that gap gets.
fit: You are an active trader with a view on the next day or the next few days
You understand daily-reset leverage and watch positions closely
notfit: You plan to buy and hold for months or years
You would be uncomfortable with a 20% or larger loss in a single week
You want a fund you do not need to monitor
risks: A large one-day drop in EUV is doubled
Volatility decay eats returns in choppy markets even if EUV ends flat
Tiny asset base and swap counterparty risk

holdings.note: Percent of net assets. The fund holds a swap, not individual stocks. See EUV for the underlying portfolio.

OPTO.about: The Tuttle Capital Photonics Income Blast ETF is the income version of FOTO. It keeps exposure to the same universe of photonics companies and adds an options strategy that sells put spreads on those stocks, with the goal of paying out the premium as weekly distributions.
OPTO.watch: The option strategy is not designed to protect you when photonics stocks fall. Distributions can include return of capital, can shrink and can be suspended, and the fund's share price can drop even while it pays out. It is also brand new and very small.
strategy: OPTO holds photonics stock exposure directly or through call options and synthetic long positions, adding up to at least 80% of net assets. Unlike a classic covered-call fund, it does not sell calls against those holdings, so it does not cap the upside on the stock sleeve in the same way.

The income comes from a separate layer of put credit spreads on the same photonics stocks. The fund sells puts close to the current price and buys cheaper puts further below. The difference in premium is the income, and the purchased puts set a known maximum loss on each spread.
Tuttle expects to pay distributions weekly but does not guarantee it. In a selloff the put spreads lose money at the same time the stock sleeve falls, so losses stack instead of offsetting.
fit: You want regular cash payouts from a photonics position
You understand that part of each payout may be your own capital coming back
You already follow weekly-pay option income ETFs and want one tied to this theme
notfit: You want maximum growth from photonics; total return can lag the plain FOTO fund
You hold in a taxable account and have not looked at how option-income distributions are taxed
You want a fund with a track record; this one launched in October 2026
risks: Put spreads add losses on top of stock losses in a falling market
Distributions are not guaranteed and may be return of capital
A 0.99% fee, the second highest on the list, and a tiny asset base

PRAM.about: The Defiance Memory & Photonics ETF is a hybrid, not a pure photonics fund. It tracks the Solactive Memory and Photonics Index: the 20 largest eligible memory and photonics companies, equal-weighted at each quarterly rebalance. Coherent, Lumentum, Zhongji Innolight and Applied Optoelectronics sit next to Micron, SK Hynix, Seagate and Western Digital.
PRAM.watch: Roughly half of PRAM is memory and data storage, so it will not track the optical stocks as closely as the pure photonics funds. The fund gets its index exposure through a total return swap, not by holding the 20 stocks directly.
strategy: Defiance pitches PRAM as the data layer of AI: the memory that stores information and the optics that move it. The index picks the 20 largest companies across those two groups and gives each roughly a 5% weight when it rebalances every quarter.

Equal weighting means a smaller name such as Applied Optoelectronics starts each quarter with the same weight as Broadcom or Micron. That gives more punch to the smaller companies than a market-cap-weighted index would.
Instead of buying the stocks, the fund holds a swap on the whole index plus a government money market fund as collateral. The issuer's holdings page shows just three line items.
fit: You want photonics and memory together in one rules-based fund
You like equal weighting so no single stock dominates
You want a published index instead of a manager's picks
notfit: You want pure photonics exposure; about half the index is memory and storage
You want the fund to hold the underlying shares directly
You want a large, heavily traded fund
risks: Memory chips are among the most cyclical parts of the semiconductor industry
All of the exposure runs through a swap with a counterparty
Small asset base

holdings.note: Index weights. The fund holds a swap on the index, not the stocks themselves.
